note: The user-facing half of the accepted-boundaries register (id, kind, userFacingText, workaround, enforcingDiagnosticCodes). This is the ONLY home for these fields -- ledger/boundaries/*.yml keeps provenance (title, ref, codeLinkedNote) and does not repeat them. Read by `npdev why <token>`. Do not hand-edit the provenance fields back in here, and do not add these fields back to the ledger.

boundaries.userFacingText: A concept or field carrying a stable `uid` is renamed by identity on ANY editing path, including a raw hand-edit through none of the authoring surfaces: change only the `name`, keep the `uid`, and a regeneration renames the live column in place with its data preserved -- no `renamedFrom` needed. `uid` is optional and generated once (`npdev migrate assign-uids` stamps one on every concept/field lacking it); a model with no uids at all behaves exactly as before, and every disciplined authoring surface (generated authoring UI, `npdev migrate rename`, `npdev_author_submit`'s AuthoringDiffGate) still captures a declared `renamedFrom` as real intent the same way it always did. Hand-editing a field's name AND deleting its `uid` still refuses -- identity was destroyed, and saying so is honest.
boundaries.workaround: Run `npdev migrate assign-uids --model <path> --write` once to stamp every concept/field with a stable identity. After that, a rename is resolved automatically by identity on ANY editing path -- no `renamedFrom`, no suggestion command, no authoring surface required. For a model that still has no uids: the pre-uid workflow is unchanged -- prefer the generated authoring UI, `npdev migrate rename`, or `npdev author submit`, or use `npdev migration diff --suggest-renames` + `npdev migrate rename --from-suggestions <file>` for a raw hand-edit.

boundaries.userFacingText: Expression-valued backfills require a dry-run preview and explicit acknowledgment -- UNLESS the platform can PROVE the expression safe: a SAFE-classified expression (a constant, a single-column copy, or a pure same-row arithmetic/comparison/logical expression with no function call) with a fresh preview showing zero failing rows auto-applies outright; a REVIEWABLE or HIGH_RISK expression (any function call, including a cross-record 'scope.*' call) auto-applies once an independent shadow run proves it -- every affected row produces a value, and a second evaluation agrees with the first. Only an expression that fails to evaluate, or disagrees across the two shadow runs, still requires the dry-run preview and explicit acknowledgment.
boundaries.workaround: Call GET /api/admin/schema-migration/expression-backfill-preview to see each candidate's risk tier and whether it will auto-apply; for anything not proven safe, review affected rows and acknowledge via the existing /acknowledge endpoint. Tune auto-apply with -Dnpdev.schema.backfill.auto-apply=none|safe|safe-and-reviewable|proven (default safe) and -Dnpdev.schema.backfill.auto-apply-max-rows=<n> (default 10000). `proven` auto-applies any risk tier, including HIGH_RISK, once the shadow proof succeeds.

boundaries.userFacingText: FK/index checking only ever adds MISSING constraints; an extra constraint your database already has is reported as informational, never proposed for removal.
boundaries.workaround: Manage extra indexes outside NPDev; NPDev respects them and never drops them. The impact report (boot log, -ImpactOnly, and ControlPanel's schema-migration/impact endpoint) includes an advisory surplus section when there is one, but it never changes the verdict.

boundaries.userFacingText: A boot with nothing to migrate (the live schema already matches this build) takes no migration lock at all and never contends another instance. A boot that DOES need to migrate and cannot obtain the lock within its budget now degrades -- rather than refusing -- when the live schema is already compatible with what this build wants, booting with a prominent warning instead of exiting. Only a boot that genuinely needs an incompatible migration and cannot obtain the lock still refuses.
boundaries.workaround: Run migration as a one-shot MIGRATE_ONLY job (Migrate-Only.ps1 / npdev.schema.lifecycle.mode=MIGRATE_ONLY) before any serving instance boots, so nothing ever contends the lock. A same-build rolling restart no longer needs this at all -- the no-op preflight already skips the lock. If two instances do race a real migration, the second waits under the real lock, extending its budget automatically while npdev_schema_history shows progress; on timeout it degrades if the live schema is already compatible (npdev.schema.lock.onTimeout=degrade, the default) or refuses if not (=refuse).

boundaries.userFacingText: This database was migrated by a newer build, and this older build boots and serves traffic normally as long as every difference is additive (an extra column this build ignores, or a whole extra table) -- logged, never touched, never a refusal. If any difference is genuinely incompatible (this build needs something missing, or an extra column is NOT NULL with no usable default), the boot still refuses, naming exactly what differs, classified as needing the newer build / needing a destructive downgrade. For a pure-superset ahead diff (nothing this build wants is missing), that residual case can also be reversed back down.
boundaries.workaround: Nothing to do for the additive case -- it boots on its own. For a genuinely incompatible difference: roll forward, use mark-done deliberately after verifying by hand (or with `npdev db verify`), or -- for a pure-superset ahead diff only -- `npdev db reverse-migrate --preview` / `--ack-token <token>` to step it back down. Run `npdev db schema-ahead --report` for the itemized diagnosis without booting the app.

boundaries.userFacingText: mark-done tells NPDev to stop trying to converge the schema and trust that you already fixed it by hand -- nothing verifies that you actually did.
boundaries.workaround: Use -ImpactOnly first to see what NPDev thinks differs, then mark done knowingly. `npdev db verify` can also check the result independently before you mark done.

boundaries.userFacingText: A refused boot can happen AFTER an earlier step already ran (e.g. an idempotent Flyway migration) -- a refusal is not guaranteed to leave the database exactly as it found it.
boundaries.workaround: Treat a refused boot as "inspect before retrying"; the schema history table records what already ran. `npdev db verify` can tell you the database's actual current state without booting.

boundaries.userFacingText: NPDev records ownership of a business table the moment its own migration creates it, before any later same-boot pass (backfill, unique-constraint tightening) can still refuse -- so a table it created can no longer end up without a record. A table that predates this (a genuinely legacy database, or one that skipped the old 'boot once with the concept present' workaround) can be adopted explicitly: GET .../ownership/preview lists which live tables would be adopted, POST .../ownership/adopt records ownership ONLY for a live table whose shape matches the model with zero difference -- never inferred, never for a table that merely shares a name. This table was not dropped because no ownership history exists is still possible, but now only for a table that genuinely was never created by this build and was never adopted.
boundaries.workaround: npdev db adopt-ownership [--apply] against a running app (preview by default, --apply to record), or boot once with the concept present the old way -- both still work.

boundaries.userFacingText: Snapshot restore can target one table, an explicit list, or every table a snapshot captured in a single call -- preflighted (nothing is written if any named table is missing live) and restored parent-before-child by foreign key order. A conflicting row (present live with different content) is still reported per table and never overwritten.
boundaries.workaround: Use the batch restore endpoint / npdev db restore --all (or --tables a,b) for more than one table; the original single-table preview/restore endpoints are unchanged for a single (snapshot, table) call.

boundaries.userFacingText: H2 to Postgres (or any engine pair) promotion is one command from either the CLI or REST: `npdev db promote --app <dir> --to <jdbcUrl>` or `POST /api/v1/admin/schema/promote` realizes the target schema (even a completely empty one), previews, applies, and verifies deeper than row counts -- never just "Postgres started successfully". A conversion hook's null-check verification can be authored declaratively (`verify: {concept, where, expect}`) instead of hand-written SQL, portable across engines by construction. It still never translates H2 SQL into Postgres SQL.
boundaries.workaround: Run `npdev db promote --app <dir> --to <jdbcUrl> --dry-run` (or POST with dryRun:true) first to preview with zero writes, then without --dry-run/dryRun to realize the schema, copy the data, and verify (row counts, per-column null counts, an order-independent content hash, and FK/index/shape parity). `npdev migrate hook-verify --input <dir> --write` converts an existing hook.json's verifySql to the declarative field automatically where the shape allows.

boundaries.userFacingText: H2 and MySQL commit DDL implicitly, so if a migration hook fails partway, its data changes roll back but any schema change it already made stays applied -- the database can end up in a state your model doesn't fully describe.
boundaries.workaround: Set -Dnpdev.schema.conversionHooks.mixedDdlVerify=split (REAL_LIFT_PLAN_2026-09-03 package A1, STOR-21) to have the platform automatically decompose a mixing hook into idempotent, journaled phases and run them, resuming safely past a real process crash on the next boot -- no human repair step. Or set =refuse to refuse the boot outright before running such a hook instead, so the mixed state can never be authored into existence; split and refuse both still refuse a statement neither can render idempotent (e.g. a bare DROP COLUMN), naming it. By default NPDev prints a warning naming the active engine before running a hook that mixes DDL with a verifySql (=warn, unchanged). Postgres and SQL Server roll back fully, so none of this is needed there.

boundaries.userFacingText: Each conversion hook runs in its own transaction; a later hook failing does not undo an earlier hook that already succeeded.
boundaries.workaround: Write every hook idempotent (ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, UPDATE ... WHERE <not-yet-converted>) so it is safe to re-run after a partial failure.

boundaries.userFacingText: This conversion references a concept or field that does not exist in the pack.
boundaries.workaround: Declare a conversions[] entry (copy/split/lookup/merge/convert/coalesce/case) instead of hand-writing convert.sql; for the uncovered case (retyping an EXISTING column in place), fall back to an operator-authored SQL hook.

boundaries.userFacingText: A destructive schema change already claimed by a conversion hook needs no separate acknowledgment token -- authoring the hook is itself the acknowledgment.
boundaries.workaround: None needed for a hook-claimed item. An unclaimed destructive item still requires the normal acknowledgment token.

boundaries.userFacingText: A forEach loop body may contain an await step, both sequentially (exactly one reachable await per iteration) and, with parallelAwait: true, in parallel across iterations (one reachable await at the loop body's top level).
boundaries.workaround: Sequential: author a forEach loop body with exactly one reachable await step. Parallel: set parallelAwait: true and put exactly one reachable await step at the loop body's top level (not nested inside a branch); other non-forEach steps may precede or follow it. A forEach nested inside a parallel forEach still needs sequential mode or a flow restructure.

boundaries.userFacingText: A field's auto-picker supports a declared filter/multi-select via field.picker, AND now a named, reusable picker configuration: declare a selectors[] entry once ({name, concept, columns, filters, orderBy, filter}) and reference it from any number of fields or band pickers via picker.selectorRef -- its display/search/order/filter are adopted wholesale, and a local filter (if also declared) AND-composes on top.
boundaries.workaround: Use field.picker.filter / field.picker.multiSelect directly for a one-off picker; use picker.selectorRef to reuse the same configuration across multiple fields/band pickers without re-declaring it each time. The older referenceSemantics.defaultFilter grammar still works unchanged.

boundaries.userFacingText: The bootstrap Super User credential is issued (default, SUPER_USER_KEY.txt), or supplied as a hash (npdev.superuser.bootstrap-key-hash, no plaintext secret needed) or a raw key above a length floor (npdev.superuser.bootstrap-key-raw). Either way it is a short-lived handoff: claim a named administrator (POST /api/admin/superuser/claim, or `npdev admin create`) and the bootstrap credential is revoked automatically. A key that was rejected because it was already claimed/revoked is told so specifically.
boundaries.workaround: Read the issued key from SUPER_USER_KEY.txt (default), or configure npdev.superuser.bootstrap-key-hash/.bootstrap-key-raw for a deployment-supplied bootstrap credential; either way, claim a named administrator promptly and the bootstrap key stops working.

boundaries.userFacingText: Concurrent writes to the same row that both pass row-level write authorization can no longer silently overwrite each other: with a real transaction manager, both writes (create and delete alike) run inside a transaction and take a real row lock, so a concurrent writer blocks; without one, both write paths compare-and-swap against the row version they just read and the loser gets an optimistic-lock conflict it can retry.
boundaries.workaround: Nothing to do -- both write paths are now safe by default in both modes (real transaction manager, or the degraded no-transaction-manager default). The only rows left unprotected are on tables created before the platform tracked row versions, where there is no version to compare against; an explicit expectedRowVersion on a write request still gives the stronger stale-authorization check.

boundaries.userFacingText: A bandPickers entry resolves either via a named panel, or -- with no panel -- via filter/multiSelect alone, which targets the band's own collection concept directly through the same reference-lookup endpoint an FK field's picker uses. Only a picker declaring neither is refused.
boundaries.workaround: Declare filter/multiSelect (with or without a panel) on a bandPickers entry; the no-panel form needs no hand-authored Selection panel at all.

boundaries.userFacingText: Bounded contexts let one app declare multiple namespaces (contexts[]/imports[]) inside a single model and database -- but a genuinely separate service (its own deployment, its own database) still needs its own app and namespace.
boundaries.workaround: Declare contexts[]/imports[] directly (see ADR-0011 and NPDevSamples/dsl-conformance-max for a real corpus example with both isolated and non-isolated contexts). Model a separate service as its own app, not as a context.

boundaries.userFacingText: query.groupBy can join up to 3 hops across concepts (same-context or cross-context); query.where and query.aggregates still name a field on the query's own base concept only.
boundaries.workaround: Declare a join directly: groupBy: ["lote.produtoId"] (1 hop) or groupBy: ["a.b.c.d"] (3 hops, at the cap); an optional context:: prefix names the final joined concept. For a chain longer than 3 hops, use a capability-backed data source instead (listConcepts + mapList + a Java capability join) -- a path beyond the cap is refused, never silently truncated.

boundaries.userFacingText: A full model reload (enabled by default) applies most changes without a restart: every panel, procedure, aggregate, and anything read through the concept gateway directly observes the new model immediately, and capabilities/bindings, the in-memory concept store, sensitive-field policy, and cron schedules all rebuild themselves in place. Two things still need a restart: a change requiring newly generated Java code (a brand-new concept's generated controller), and a change to something the generated CRUD REST surface itself caches once (a new invariant rule, a new capability binding, or a new field's CRUD-write reachability).
boundaries.workaround: Use POST /api/admin/runtime/metadata-hotswap/model-reload (SUPERUSER-gated) for a live reload -- most changes take effect immediately. Restart the app (~30s) only when the change adds a new concept (needs generated code), a new invariant/capability binding, or when a newly added field needs to be CRUD-writable through the generated REST surface specifically. Opt out entirely with npdev.runtime.hotswap.full-model-reload-enabled=false.

boundaries.userFacingText: Any request for 'at most N rows' works on every supported engine: your code asks for a capped read as a whole statement, and each engine applies the cap the way it actually can (a LIMIT suffix where one exists, SELECT TOP n on SQL Server). There is no dialect question left that one engine cannot answer.
boundaries.workaround: Nothing to do -- every caller that asks for a row cap gets a whole statement every engine can run, and a non-positive cap is refused on every engine. A fragment-level row-suffix method is deliberately not offered: if you ever need a cap-shaped piece of SQL, ask the dialect for a complete statement instead of assembling one from fragments.

boundaries.userFacingText: Both plugin:java-source and plugin:java-controller mounts run OS-process-isolated (a separate child JVM per worker, IPC dispatch) with an enforced OS-level ceiling (default 512MB memory / 50% CPU on Windows Job Objects or Linux cgroups) -- each is admission-checked at generation and boot against a bytecode denylist AND bounded at runtime (SEC-3/5/6/7 for java-source, SEC-9 for java-controller). A pooled worker no longer runs on the host's own full classpath -- only the entries a real generated app's plugin classes and their runtime dependencies need -- and a class outside the plugin's own reserved package, or on the same escape denylist the bytecode gate already enforces, is refused at class-load time inside the child even if constructed dynamically at runtime rather than referenced statically. On Linux, the child additionally runs under an OS-level network and filesystem sandbox (private network namespace, read-only system paths) -- an outbound socket attempt fails at the OS layer even with the classloader disabled. Windows has no equivalent OS-level sandbox, so containment there rests on the restricted classpath and classloader denylist alone.
boundaries.workaround: The OS-level ceiling and containment are on by default for both mount kinds; retune via npdev.runtime.plugin-ipc-pool.memory-limit-mb / .cpu-rate-percent if a real plugin's workload needs more headroom, or npdev.runtime.plugin-ipc-pool.sandbox=off to disable the Linux network/filesystem sandbox specifically. Isolation is unconditional for both -- only mount plugin code you trust the SOURCE of; admission checks escapes, it does not review business logic. A plugin that busy-loops inside its own bounded, sandboxed process without exceeding the memory/CPU ceiling is still bounded but not stopped early.

boundaries.userFacingText: H2Local (embedded file) databases now default to H2's own AUTO_SERVER mode: the first process serves the file over TCP and every later process connects through it instead of racing the file, so a rolling restart's brief overlap boots both processes with no wait and no refusal. The older lock-and-wait behavior (another process holds the file, boot waits then refuses on timeout) is still available as an explicit opt-out.
boundaries.workaround: Nothing to do -- AUTO_SERVER is on by default for H2Local. To opt back into the wait-then-refuse behavior instead (e.g. to keep only one process ever serving), set npdev.h2local.autoServer=false or name AUTO_SERVER=FALSE explicitly in the JDBC URL; under that mode, raise -Dnpdev.h2local.bootLock.waitSeconds=<seconds> if restarts legitimately take longer than the default 30s budget.
